clue.text: Justify precious landscape painter

parts.note: to aver is to affirm or assert as true, a sense close to justify
precious in the sense of affected or mannered is camp

explanation.surface: Someone defends a dainty, overrefined painter of country scenes.
explanation.definitionFit: Hendrick Avercamp was a Dutch Golden Age painter famous for winter landscapes with skaters.

clue.text: Very old record one put on for foxy character

parts.note: an LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: An ancient recording is played for a cunning person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on' only joins the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Volpone, Italian for 'big fox', is the cunning title character of Ben Jonson's comedy.

clue.text: Hope inspired, idealistically romantic

parts.note: the novelist Anthony Hope invented this imaginary kingdom, whose name now stands for any idealised romantic setting

explanation.surface: Optimism was stirred, in a dreamy, starry-eyed way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hope' looks like the feeling but is the author Anthony Hope, who set The Prisoner of Zenda in this made-up Central European kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Hope's fictional kingdom gave English an adjective for any romantically idealised little realm.

clue.text: Novel heroine from the Middle East, inter alia

indicators.note: Latin inter means between, so a piece is placed between the letters of the next word

parts.note: ME is the usual abbreviation for the Middle East

explanation.surface: A fictional heroine hails from the Middle East, among other places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inter alia' reads as the Latin phrase 'among other things', but 'inter' (between) is the container signal acting on the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Fielding's last novel takes its title from its heroine, the long-suffering wife of Captain Booth.

clue.text: Caused by Master's comic gift?

parts.note: a gift is a present, and what a comic gift causes is mirth; the Master was Noel Coward's nickname, and this is one of his comedies

explanation.surface: What the Master's talent for comedy produces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Master' was the playwright Noel Coward's nickname; the clue reads the title of his 1939 comedy as 'a gift' plus 'what comedy causes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel Coward, known as the Master, wrote this comedy; its title splits into a gift and the mirth a comic produces.

clue.text: Namely poor, and backward, nevertheless a name featuring in four of the Histories

definitions.text: a name featuring in four of the Histories

parts.note: SC abbreviates Latin scilicet, meaning namely

indicators.note: backward tells us the word before it is read from right to left

explanation.surface: Someone poor and slow, yet whose name turns up in several of Shakespeare's history plays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Namely' is the Latin scilicet, abbreviated in footnotes; 'backward' turns the word 'poor'. The four plays are Richard II, both parts of Henry IV and Henry V.
explanation.definitionFit: Scroop is a family name borne by characters in Richard II, Henry IV Part 1 and 2 and Henry V.

clue.text: Girl supports second friend for composer

indicators.note: in a down clue the piece that supports sits below, so the girl's name comes last

parts.note: a chum is a friend
Ann is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl backs up her second friend for the sake of a composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Schumann was a German Romantic composer of songs, piano music and symphonies.

clue.text: Sort of theatre misused in opera

indicators.note: something misused is put to the wrong order of use, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A kind of theatre is badly handled in an opera production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misused' rearranges the letters of IN OPERA.
explanation.definitionFit: An outdoor theatre stages plays under the sky rather than in a building.

clue.text: Undisciplined Leone epic: a sort of prehistoric Western, perhaps?

definitions.text: a sort of prehistoric Western, perhaps?

indicators.note: undisciplined letters are out of order, so the following words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Sergio Leone's sprawling epic is imagined as a cowboy film set in prehistoric times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undisciplined' rearranges LEONE EPIC. Sergio Leone directed spaghetti Westerns; the definition imagines a Western set in this geological epoch.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pliocene, older spelling Pleiocene, is the geological epoch before the Pleistocene, so prehistoric.

clue.text: Rumoured pilgrim science-fiction writer

indicators.note: something rumoured is passed by word of mouth, so we want a word that is spoken like this

parts.note: the Clerk of Oxenford is one of the pilgrims in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales

explanation.surface: Gossip about a pilgrim who writes science fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech 'clerk' is said 'clark'.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur C. Clarke wrote 2001: A Space Odyssey and other classic science fiction.

clue.text: Playwright gives point there, to good English

parts.note: E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A dramatist points out a spot and gives it to a fine Englishman.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir George Etherege was a Restoration dramatist, author of The Man of Mode.

clue.text: I interrupt German poet to indicate French fabulist

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into, so I goes into the middle of the next piece

parts.note: Theodor Fontane was a German poet and novelist

explanation.surface: A speaker cuts in on a German poet to point out a French writer of fables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to indicate' joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean de La Fontaine was the seventeenth-century French author of verse fables.

clue.text: "A more humane never did in Japan exist"

definitions.text: "A more humane never did in Japan exist"

parts.words: "A more humane never did in Japan exist"
parts.note: a line sung by the title character of a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta; the missing word after 'humane' is the answer

explanation.surface: A line praising a ruler as the kindest Japan has known.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation has a gap after 'humane': fill in the speaker's own title from Gilbert and Sullivan's operetta.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mikado, the Japanese emperor, sings this line about himself in Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera.

clue.text: Far-seeing novelist, never translated

indicators.note: translated means turned into another form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A visionary writer whose work was never put into another language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translated' rearranges NEVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Verne foresaw submarines and space travel in his novels, so he was far-seeing.

clue.text: "The shade of some dead accountant, with pen in ear, would flit by me" (Charles Lamb)

definitions.text: "The shade of some dead accountant, with pen in ear, would flit by me" (Charles Lamb)

parts.words: "The shade of some dead accountant, with pen in ear, would flit by me" (Charles Lamb)
parts.note: Lamb's essay on the South-Sea House has a word before 'pen' describing the ghostly pen; that dropped word is the answer

explanation.surface: Charles Lamb pictures the ghost of a long-dead clerk drifting past him.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation from Lamb's essay The South-Sea House drops one word: 'with ____ pen in ear'.
explanation.definitionFit: The ghost's pen is imagined, seen only in a vision, which is what the missing adjective says.

clue.text: Reseating arrangement for Hornung piece

indicators.note: an arrangement puts things in a new order, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A new seating plan for a performance of a work by Hornung.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrangement' rearranges RESEATING. E. W. Hornung, creator of Raffles, also wrote stories about the bushranger Stingaree.
explanation.definitionFit: Stingaree is a book of stories by E. W. Hornung about an Australian outlaw of that name.

clue.text: Excellent as Barrie's butler

explanation.surface: Praise for J. M. Barrie's manservant.
explanation.walkthrough: J. M. Barrie's play The Admirable Crichton is about a capable butler.
explanation.definitionFit: Excellent means deserving praise; Barrie's butler Crichton is called this in the play's title.

clue.text: Gothic stepdame in unseemly rush

indicators.note: Gothic in the old sense of barbarous or crude, so the letters are roughly treated and rearranged

explanation.surface: A wicked stepmother from a Gothic novel dashes off in an undignified hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gothic' rearranges STEPDAME; it seems to describe a villainous stepmother from horror fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: A stampede is a sudden headlong charge of a crowd or herd, a disorderly dash.

clue.text: He roomed with Aloysius at Oxford

definitions.text: He roomed with Aloysius at Oxford

parts.words: He roomed with Aloysius at Oxford
parts.note: Aloysius is the teddy bear carried around Oxford by a young aristocrat in Waugh's Brideshead Revisited

explanation.surface: A student shared lodgings with a friend at university.
explanation.walkthrough: Aloysius sounds like a fellow student but is a teddy bear: Lord Sebastian Flyte carries him everywhere in Evelyn Waugh's Brideshead Revisited.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Sebastian Flyte, in Brideshead Revisited, kept his teddy bear Aloysius with him at Oxford.

clue.text: Country musician heard

indicators.note: heard means we want a word that is said like the musician's name

parts.note: Benjamin Britten was an English composer

explanation.surface: A country-music performer is listened to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' suggests a music genre, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain is a nation, the island holding England, Scotland and Wales.

clue.text: Tickle Calliope, for example ()

explanation.surface: Someone teases one of the Muses.
explanation.walkthrough: Calliope is the Muse of epic poetry, so she is a Muse.
explanation.definitionFit: To tickle someone is to entertain them; Calliope is one of the nine Muses of Greek myth.

clue.text: Coningsby's role model gets first-class return to port

parts.note: Sidon is an ancient Phoenician port in Lebanon

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the piece before is read backwards

parts.note: A1 is first-class, written here as the letters AI

explanation.surface: Someone sails home first class to a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns the first-class letters round; Sidon is in modern Lebanon. Coningsby is Disraeli's novel, not a person to look up.
explanation.definitionFit: In Disraeli's novel Coningsby, the wise Jewish financier Sidonia is the hero's mentor and model.

clue.text: Uninteresting publicity for spirits

parts.note: dry writing is dull or uninteresting
ads are advertisements, publicity

explanation.surface: Boring advertising for alcoholic drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Dryads are tree nymphs of Greek myth, nature spirits.

clue.text: Sash from 12 is medieval black magic

parts.note: 12 across is set in Japan, and the obi is the Japanese sash
M is an abbreviation for medieval

explanation.surface: A Japanese sash turns out to be a tool of dark sorcery.
explanation.walkthrough: The 12 refers to the answer to 12 across, the Gilbert and Sullivan operetta set in Japan.
explanation.definitionFit: Obeah, or obiism, is a West Indian form of sorcery or witchcraft.

clue.text: On her own admission it was "the drink, the drink that did it for her

definitions.text: On her own admission it was "the drink, the drink that did it for her

parts.words: On her own admission it was "the drink, the drink that did it for her
parts.note: a Shakespeare queen cries 'O, the drink, the drink! I am poison'd' as she dies

explanation.surface: A woman confesses that alcohol was her downfall.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's mother dies of the poisoned cup meant for her son, crying 'the drink, the drink!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Gertrude in Hamlet drinks poisoned wine and names the drink as her killer.

clue.text: Foot of a peasant fractured

indicators.note: something fractured is broken up, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A farm worker's broken foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fractured' rearranges A PEASANT; 'Foot' is a metrical unit, not part of the body.
explanation.definitionFit: An anapaest is a metrical foot of two short syllables and one long.

clue.text: Some attached to vestment in ancient kingdom

indicators.note: attached to means the first piece is joined on after the second

parts.note: an alb is a white priestly vestment
any can mean some, as in 'have you any?'

explanation.surface: A few things pinned to a priest's robe in an old realm.
explanation.definitionFit: Albany was the old name of the northern part of Scotland, a former realm.

clue.text: Twain's was to be seen at Camelot

definitions.text: Twain's was to be seen at Camelot

parts.words: Twain's was to be seen at Camelot
parts.note: Mark Twain wrote of a time-travelling New Englander at King Arthur's court

explanation.surface: Something of Mark Twain's appeared at King Arthur's court.
explanation.walkthrough: Twain's novel A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court sends an American to Camelot.
explanation.definitionFit: Twain's hero is an American from Connecticut, the kind of New Englander called this.

clue.text: Princely refugee from Happy Valley

parts.note: Samuel Johnson's tale concerns an Abyssinian prince who escapes a secluded valley of contentment

explanation.surface: A royal escapee flees a contented paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: In Johnson's tale the prince escapes the Happy Valley, where Abyssinian princes are confined, to seek happiness in the world.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson's Rasselas is the prince of Abyssinia who flees the Happy Valley.
